title: Cross-Layer TopK: Dynamically Allocating Sparsity Across Layers in Transcoders
summary: Cross-Layer Transcoders (CLTs) decompose the activations of large language models into human-interpretable features and trace how these features interact across layers to form circuits, making them a key tool for mechanistic interpretability. However, training CLTs effectively and efficiently is hard. Beyond the usual trade-off between sparsity and reconstruction quality, a CLT has to model all layers at once, which adds a further challenge. The common JumpReLU recipe controls sparsity only indirectly through a penalty, while the direct extension of TopK selects a fixed number of latents in every layer. Yet reconstruction difficulty differs widely across layers, and intermediate layers are much harder than others, so giving every layer the same budget is suboptimal. We propose Cross-Layer TopK, which sets a single L0 budget for the whole model and dynamically allocates it across layers during training. In a comparison with JumpReLU and other TopK variants on Qwen3-8B-Base, this gives lower FVU while using 20% fewer active latents than JumpReLU. The better reconstruction carries over to circuit tracing, yielding more complete circuits with higher replacement and completeness scores. The fixed per-token budget of Cross-Layer TopK also makes it easy to pair with sparse decoding, which cuts both computation and communication and gives a 2.9x speedup per training step. We further show that Cross-Layer TopK follows scaling laws in both latent size and sparsity. We have open-sourced the weights of our CLT at https://huggingface.co/ByteDance-Seed/Cross-Layer-TopK-CLT.

title: Integrating MBSE Principles with AI to Improve the Quality of Requirements in SMEs Context
summary: Model-Based Systems Engineering (MBSE) is a promising approach to improve systems engineering practices, particularly by enhancing requirement management, traceability, and early validation and verification (V\&V). However, its adoption remains challenging, especially for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), which often lack structured processes and solutions adapted to their scale and constraints. Our goal is to propose a lightweight MBSE methodology tailored to the needs and constraints of SMEs. This paper focuses specifically on requirements refinement, traceability, and early V\&V. The approach integrates MBSE principles with artificial intelligence-assisted analysis to improve requirements quality while remaining compatible with existing tools and practices. A proof of concept is developed and applied in an industrial case study to evaluate the feasibility of the approach. The results demonstrate how early V\&V activities can be supported within an SME context, while improving traceability across engineering artifacts. These findings highlight the potential of a lightweight, integrated MBSE approach to support the progressive adoption of MBSE in SMEs, thereby improving overall engineering efficiency.

title: Controllable Molecule Generation via Sparse Representation Editing: An Interpretability-Driven Perspective
summary: Controllable molecule generation is crucial for diverse scientific applications, such as drug discovery and materials design. While large language models (LLMs) show great promise, their dense and entangled representations impede precise control over the generation of molecules with bespoke substructures or properties. To address this, we propose Sparse Representation Editing (SpaRE), an interpretability-driven framework for fine-grained and precise control in LLM-based molecule generation. The crux of SpaRE is to learn an overcomplete sparse feature space that disentangles LLM representations into a compact set of latent features corresponding to chemically meaningful concepts. Within this space, we can directly manipulate these concept-aligned latent features to achieve (1) local control, by generating target atoms and functional groups at specified positions; and (2) global control, by customizing the overall structural and physicochemical properties within defined ranges. In this way, our framework advances interpretability from post-hoc analysis to actionable generative control. Experiments show that SpaRE can generate chemically desirable molecules under complex constraints in real-world scenarios, while offering mechanistic insights for quantitative structure-property analysis. The code and demo are available at https://github.com/WanyuGroup/ICML2026_SpaRE.

title: Audiovisual Disparities in VR: Impact on Spatial Perception
comments: 2025 IEEE International Symposium on Mixed and Augmented Reality (ISMAR)
summary: Virtual reality (VR) experiences often leverage rich and spatialized multimodal environments to increase immersion and engagement. This demands a consistent spatial perception of audiovisual stimuli, since perceived discrepancies can disrupt the sense of presence. In this work, we investigate the consequences of two types of spatial audiovisual disparities: true disparity, where there is a measurable spatial offset between auditory and visual cues, and perceptual disparity, where users report misalignment despite cues being colocated. Unlike most previous studies that employed controlled but simplified experimental setups, our research focuses on complex, realistic VR environments, allowing us to assess the actual implications for VR content design. Our experiments indicate that users are highly sensitive to true audiovisual disparities in controlled environments, detecting even minor misalignments. However, when engaged in additional tasks within realistic settings, their ability to notice such discrepancies diminishes significantly. We also observed that previously found perceptual disparities persist in complex audiovisual environments. However, we identify self-initiated head rotations as a key factor; its absence prevents the effect entirely. We hope our findings offer practical insights for designing more immersive and perceptually coherent VR experiences.
comment: 2025 IEEE International Symposium on Mixed and Augmented Reality (ISMAR)

title: DUET: Dual-Sparse Inference for Block Diffusion Language Models
summary: Diffusion language models (DLMs) enable parallel token generation through iterative denoising, yet their inference remains costly due to repeated attention over a growing historical prefix and repeated processing of the entire current generation block. Historical attention becomes increasingly expensive as generation progresses, while all current-block positions are propagated through the Transformer at every denoising step even though only a small fraction are typically resolved at that step. In this paper, we introduce Duet, a training-free dual-sparse inference framework that addresses these challenges through prefix Key-Value (KV) sparsity and early query sparsity, respectively. Specifically, Duet exploits the concentration and cross-step stability of historical attention within each generation block to construct a compact historical KV subset that is reused across denoising steps. For query sparsity, Duet predicts update positions from shallow representations and propagates only the corresponding queries through the suffix Transformer layers, avoiding deep computation at positions unlikely to be updated in the current step. Experiments show that Duet maintains competitive accuracy while achieving 1.34$\times$/2.83$\times$ end-to-end/per-step speedups on LLaDA2.1-mini and 2.41$\times$/4.72$\times$ on SDAR-8B-Chat-b32 at a 32K context length.

title: MM-DyGraph: A Dataset, Benchmark, and Model for Multimodal Dynamic Graphs
summary: Multimodal dynamic graphs are pervasive in real-world applications, where nodes and edges are accompanied by multimodal signals, including text and images. Despite their practical importance, benchmarks and methods that explicitly study multimodal learning in dynamic graphs remain scarce, hindering the full understanding and effective utilization of multimodal information for downstream tasks. To address this gap, we introduce MM-DyGraph, to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark for multimodal dynamic graph learning, consisting of diverse real-world datasets with fine-grained temporal graph evolution and rich multimodal attributes. MM-DyGraph provides three evaluation tasks to comprehensively assess model performance in dynamic settings. We benchmark representative state-of-the-art dynamic graph methods and reveal that naive feature concatenation yields target-level inconsistencies: multimodal inputs benefit certain prediction targets while harming others. This observation indicates that the modality informativeness depends on the specific prediction target over time. Building on these observations, we propose a Target-aware Spatial-Temporal Multimodal Fusion (TST-MF) framework, which jointly conditions multimodal fusion on the prediction target and spatial-temporal relations, enabling context-adaptive cross-modal interplay for target-specific representations. Extensive experiments over diverse datasets and tasks show that TST-MF delivers robust and competitive performance, achieving clear gains in multimodal settings.

title: Attaining Optimal Values under Sure Constraints
comments: 61 pages, 6 figures. Complete proofs included. Corresponding author: Takuto Yamauchi
summary: A game may have, for each target below its value, a finite controller meeting that target, yet no finite controller attaining the value itself. We study finite stochastic games with a hard specification that must hold on every supported execution, including paths of probability zero. Max uses a pure finite controller; Min may use any pure public-history strategy. We distinguish three numerical questions: can a supplied target be met, can the unspecified optimum be attained, and what is one exact value? For explicit hard and Boolean soft Streett conditions, the strict and non-strict supplied-threshold problems are coNP-complete, attainment of the unsupplied supremum is $\mathrm P^{\mathrm{NP}}$-complete, and one exact reduced fraction is $\mathrm{FP}^{\mathrm{NP}}$-complete under polynomial metric reductions. The proofs preserve both the value and its finite attainability when fixing a single opponent, and encode adaptive queries without computing unknown subgame values. The same construction yields matching value-comparison and exact-output lower bounds for ordinary stochastic Streett games with unrestricted randomized history strategies. We also bound the memory needed for optimal finite implementations for arbitrary Muller hard conditions and rational rewards in $[0,1]$ determined by infinitely recurring states. One controller is sure from the entire original sure region and attains at every finitely attained start, with no attainment premise on the other states. For $n$ states in that region it uses $2^{O(n\log(n+1))}Q(1+\log R)$ modes, where $Q$ is the product of the least common denominators of full original chance rows sourced in that sure region and $R$ clears all reward values. Its joint dependence on $Q$ and $R$ is worst-case sharp at each fixed $n\ge6$ when $Q,R\ge2$. Optimal dependence on arena size and efficient general synthesis are not resolved here.
comment: 61 pages, 6 figures. Complete proofs included. Corresponding author: Takuto Yamauchi

title: On the convergence of Lattice Boltzmann method for advection-diffusion equation with intermediate scaling
summary: The purpose of this article is to study the convergence of a lattice Boltzmann method (LBM) for a simple diffusion equation. The LBM is proven to be stable and consistent in some sense, so that convergence results may be obtained. The approach is similar to asymptotic analysis in the literature, although the schemes are also studied for intermediate time scalings. Usually, LBM are used in the range of acoustic regime, where $δ$t ___ $δ$x, or in diffusive scaling, with $δ$t ___ $δ$x 2 . In this work, we study any intermediate scaling $δ$t ___ $δ$x 1+r with r $\in$]0; 1]. The goal is to prove that this scaling is capable of approximating an advection-diffusion equation, provided the relaxation rate is chosen in accordance with $δ$x. Convergence results are established and match the previously known results in the diffusive regime. The second objective is to prove that several choices for the initial condition are suitable for convergence. In particular, the usual choice of equilibrium distribution at initial time guarantees that the LBM scheme yields an accurate approximation of the macroscopic quantities.

title: Practical Non-Stationary Graph Gaussian Processes
summary: Gaussian processes on graphs provide a principled framework for prediction and uncertainty estimation, but modelling heterogeneous networks often requires balancing flexibility against parameter complexity. Variability at a node may reflect useful signal that should propagate through the network, unreliable measurements whose influence should be suppressed, or a mixture of both. We introduce Variance-Coupled Gaussian Processes (VCGPs), which use a positive auxiliary signal to modulate graph interactions through a single learned coupling exponent. The exponent controls how strongly high-variability nodes propagate or attenuate information, while a cluster-wise extension accommodates different regimes within the same graph. Under stated structural assumptions, we characterize the unique stationary-rescaling point of the basic family, where correlations match those of a stationary graph kernel while node-dependent variances remain. Experiments on traffic, air-quality and weather datasets show competitive prediction and uncertainty estimation relative to stationary and per-node non-stationary baselines, with the largest gains on networks requiring multiple coupling regimes. Stationary correlations after variance rescaling remain sufficient on some data, and performance depends on the auxiliary signal and model selection.

title: Topology as a Design Variable: Joint Architecture-Sizing Optimization for SRAM
summary: SRAM's power-performance-area-stability trade-off depends on bitcell topology, a discrete architectural choice that interacts non-separably with continuous transistor sizing. However, no open-source SRAM tool treats topology as an optimizable variable. OpenRAM generates SRAM layouts but performs no optimization, while OpenYield supports high-fidelity evaluation but restricts optimization to scalar sizing of a fixed 6T cell. OpenYieldV2 closes this gap through three integrated contributions. First, a fully parameterized compiler generates complete 6T and 10T SRAM macros with peripheral circuits and replica-bitline self-timing, enabling topology comparison under identical simulation conditions. Second, a few-shot TabPFN surrogate learns topology-dependent PPA responses with limited full-macro SPICE samples. Third, a coarse-to-refined multi-objective optimizer combines global exploration of discrete architectural choices with local refinement of continuous transistor sizes. Experiments across varying design conditions reveal a topology decision boundary that shifts with operating constraints rather than following a fixed design rule. Jointly optimizing across this boundary improves hypervolume by up to 17.3\% over the strongest single-topology baseline. OpenYieldV2 is open-source to support reproducible SRAM design research.

title: Green500: Adventure in Qualifying a Cluster
summary: Energy effciency has become a key metric for evaluating High Performance Computing (HPC) systems, as reflected by the Green500 ranking. However, energy effciency alone does not capture the full environmental impact of an HPC cluster. Using the Kuma cluster at EPFL, we report on two Green500 measurement campaigns at Level 2 and Level 3, and extend this analysis to a full carbon footprint assessment using the MITSI life-cycle based methodology. GPU power capping experiments show that energy effciency peaks at 450 W, achieving an 11% performance loss offset by a 20% reduction in energy consumption. When embodied emissions are accounted for, the optimal power cap for carbon effciency shifts to 500 W under Switzerland's low-carbon electrical grid, revealing a tension between minimizing usage and embodied contributions. We discuss the challenges of generalizing this approach into a broader carbon-based HPC ranking, and argue that moving beyond energy effciency is both necessary and feasible.

title: Rethinking MoE Load Balancing as Feedback Control
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) training is often not stationary: the data mixture changes at curriculum boundaries, when a model is continually pretrained into a new domain, or when the corpus is refreshed. Routing is learned against the current mixture, so each such change disrupts the per-expert load the router had converged to, and existing balancing methods have only been evaluated on stationary data. We rethink load balancing as a feedback control problem, in which the deviation of each expert's load from its fair share is the control error and the per-expert routing bias is the control input, and define a family of controllers, the PID-Balancer, from the proportional, integral, and derivative terms of classical PID control. Two widely used methods belong to this family: the auxiliary balancing loss behaves like a proportional controller, and the loss-free bias update is an integral controller acting on the sign of the error. Reading the router as a static map with a one-step delay, we show that the integral term is the only one that both removes persistent imbalance and averages out the step-to-step fluctuation of the measured load, whereas the proportional and derivative terms pass or amplify that fluctuation into the routing bias. We therefore adopt PID (I), the pure-integral member of the family with a single gain. Two settings are evaluated: (i) training an OLMoE backbone from scratch with 16 to 64 experts per layer, through a mid-run mixture switch, and (ii) continual pretraining of the released OLMoE-1B-7B on a new corpus. PID (I) holds balance before the shift and restores it more tightly afterwards than either the auxiliary loss or loss-free balancing, at comparable perplexity.

title: TwinHash: Two-Sided Object Identity Management for Time- and Energy-Efficient Agentic Workflows
summary: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) services interleave large language model (LLM) generation with external tool execution, and increasingly rely on search-based workflows that repeatedly revisit shared reasoning states and computations. These patterns create substantial redundancy across tool outputs, LLM responses, and key-value (KV) prefixes, yet existing serving systems primarily optimize shared prompt prefixes, while naive input-keyed caching is unsafe when identical requests produce different outputs. We present TwinHash, a unified object management architecture that assigns each object an input-side hash key to recognize repeated requests and an output-side content fingerprint to validate and locate stored state, complemented by type-specific reuse guards that preserve correctness and response diversity. A software object identity table maintains reusable objects across requests and trajectories, while a hardware object placement table tracks their residency across hierarchical memory tiers so that evicted state can be retrieved rather than recomputed. Across seven agent frameworks and five benchmark suites, reuse follows workflow structure more than benchmark identity. TwinHash serves up to 81% of tool outputs wherever deterministic tool reads recur, and up to 92% of LLM responses in search-based frameworks. Retrieving an evicted KV-prefix from DRAM reduces TTFT by up to 5.6x on Qwen3-32B, with greater gains projected for larger dense models. Under search-based frameworks, TwinHash reduces end-to-end wall-clock time by up to 87% and measured task energy by up to 81% over a prefix-cached baseline, while a per-key serving cap controls the quality-reuse trade-off in adaptive search. These results demonstrate that unified identity, safety, and placement management can convert structural redundancy in emerging agentic workflows into substantial serving-efficiency gains.

title: Zero-Query Transferable Pretend Benign Attacks with Amortized Online Generation for Cooperative Perception
summary: Cooperative perception enables an ego agent to acquire information from collaborators beyond its own sensors' reach. Yet, the most beneficial messages are often the hardest to verify from local observations. Pretend Benign (PB) exploits this asymmetry by targeting regions with weak local verifiability and applying multi-objective perturbations, making harmful feature changes appear to be benign assistance. However, PB is victim-dependent: selecting regions and optimizing perturbations require the victim model's architecture, parameters, and gradients, limiting transfer to unseen victims. A transferable attack must capture properties shared across cooperative detection models rather than those specific to one network. We address this by building a victim-agnostic attack from a heterogeneous ensemble of surrogate models and encoding its capabilities in a reusable dictionary to reduce per-message generation cost. Specifically, Transferable Pretend Benign (TrPB) transfers PB's region selection criterion and multi-objective perturbation strategy across heterogeneous surrogates to construct an offline attack. We further propose RT-TrPB, which encodes transferable regions and perturbation patterns into a region predictor and reusable perturbation dictionary, amortizing per-message attack generation. Experiments on widely used cooperative perception benchmarks show that RT-TrPB bypasses the consensus-based defenses ROBOSAC and FLD with success rates approaching 100% and generates each perturbation in under 56 ms. To counter PB-style attacks masquerading as benign collaboration, we also propose STTrust, which verifies received messages using spatial and temporal consistency and incorporates identity-level trust. STTrust detects over 90% of PB-style attacks and restores perception performance to near the attack-free level.

title: Forecasting cumulative intraoperative hypotension burden: patient-disjoint evaluation of quantile boosting and alert policies
summary:
Background: Binary hypotension forecasts do not describe the depth and duration of future low pressure. Burden forecasts may support graded early warning, but better forecast scores need not yield more useful alerts.
  Objective: To evaluate conditional quantiles of the next 15-minute mean arterial pressure (MAP) deficit below 65 mmHg and distinguish forecasting performance from episode-warning performance.
  Methods: Public VitalDB numeric arterial MAP was reduced to 10-second medians without forward filling. Subject-disjoint training, validation and test splits included 70,402, 14,270 and 15,575 labeled windows. We compared climatology, calibrated persistence, last-MAP-only boosting, and direct and residual quantile boosting, with and without additional MAP-history features. Patient-weighted pinball loss and subject-bootstrap intervals evaluated forecasting. Validation selected alert thresholds before a hash-recorded test evaluation.
  Results: In the test split, the prespecified residual-versus-persistence comparison at the 90th percentile yielded losses of 2.256 and 2.900 mmHg-min, respectively (difference -0.644; 95% interval -0.814 to -0.487). Direct prediction achieved 2.196, and direct prediction with additional MAP features achieved 2.193. Episode-warning results were sensitive to the alert rule and operating threshold.
  Conclusions: This retrospective benchmark separates burden-forecast skill from warning-policy performance. Findings support further study of direct burden estimation; they do not establish patient benefit, prospective reliability or transportability beyond the source hospital.

title: Navigating Complexity: A User-Centered Evaluation of Project Management Tools
summary: In the age of digital transformation, companies are increasingly relying on specialized software to manage the complexity of projects. However, when selecting tools, features and costs often take precedence over user experience (UX), leading to low adoption rates, user frustration, and project delays. This study empirically evaluates the user experience of leading project management tools (Jira, Trello, Monday.com, Asana, and Microsoft Project) across various project scales using a mixed methods approach. The System Usability Scale (SUS) was used as the primary quantitative instrument, with data collected from 141 experienced professionals via online questionnaires. The results reveal a significant trade-off between functionality and usability. Trello achieved the highest SUS score (77.5), indicating a superior user experience for small projects and agile teams, while Microsoft Project scored the lowest (51.2), suggesting significant usability challenges despite its robust features. Jira demonstrated a balanced profile, offering powerful features with manageable complexity. Statistical analyses confirmed that the choice of the optimal tool is highly context dependent, with team size and project complexity influencing UX outcomes. The findings underscore that UX is not a secondary feature but a critical success factor for software acceptance and project effectiveness. This study provides an evidence-based framework for aligning tool selection with the project context, offers practitioners actionable insights, and identifies design opportunities for software developers.

title: Path Isolation and Reachability in Surface-Embedded Graphs with Restricted Cycle and Cut Structure
summary:
We study the reachability problem in directed surface-embedded graphs under two structural restrictions, using isolating weight assignments.
  First, we consider graphs whose underlying undirected embeddings contain at most polynomially many simple surface non-separating cycles. We develop a polynomially bounded, logspace-computable skew-symmetric edge-weight assignment with nonzero circulation around every simple cycle. This yields an unambiguous logspace (UL) upper bound for directed reachability. The construction also gives an SPL upper bound for bipartite perfect matching in the corresponding undirected graph class.
  Second, for $g$-genus directed graphs admitting a balanced hierarchical genus decomposition with $O(\log n)$ crossing edges at every partition, we obtain an unambiguous $O(\log g \cdot \log n)$-space bound for reachability. Our approach combines path-isolating weights for lower-genus subgraphs using polynomially bounded FKS hashing refinements at successive merging levels.

title: Model-based learning for DoA estimation and array calibration via continuous sparse recovery
summary: Direction of arrival (DoA) estimation, a classical signal processing problem, has experienced renewed interest with the advent of integrated sensing and communication (ISAC). While decades of research have yielded highly accurate DoA estimators, hardware impairments have frequently been neglected, despite degrading both DoA estimation accuracy and downstream communication performance in ISAC systems. This work introduces a joint array calibration and DoA estimation method based on the simultaneous orthogonal matching pursuit (SOMP) algorithm, following the model-based machine learning paradigm. The proposed method enables the calibration of antenna arrays subject to severe gain-phase and antenna location impairments through projected gradient descent (PGD), with either supervised or unsupervised objectives. Additionally, DoA estimation is enhanced by extending SOMP to continuous dictionaries via PGD refinement steps. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method enables efficient hardware impairment compensation, even without labeled samples, while outperforming conventional sparse recovery and subspace-based DoA estimation baselines.

title: Nudging Decision Models: Do Digital Nudges Steer Fast, Generation-Free AI Agents?
summary: LLM-based agents increasingly automate business and consumer tasks but are slow and expensive. Decision models, a new class that chooses among options without generating text, are far faster and less costly. Developers call them "System One models," referencing dual process theory. We ask whether such models can be steered by digital nudges online and whether, as the theory predicts, automatic nudges affect them more than reflective ones. We adapted an online shopping experiment, previously run with humans and LLM agents, to three decision models (Jev, Decision-1, d1). Across 600 runs per model, they chose a preselected default in 97.5-99.9% and a product with social influence information in 75-96% of choices, versus 47-49% in the control. All responded more strongly to the automatic nudge, the opposite of what has been reported for reasoning-capable LLM agents. We provide first evidence that non-generative decision models are susceptible to digital nudges in a System 1 pattern, implying agent-type-specific nudge effects.

title: Reconciling European Electricity Data with Diffusion Priors Learned from Observations Alone
summary: The ENTSO-E Transparency Platform publishes generation, load, and cross-border power flows for European bidding zones. The values carry undocumented errors and violate energy conservation, and data reconciliation consists in correcting them to satisfy that balance. In this work, we formulate data reconciliation as Bayesian inference. Classical methods implicitly take a uniform prior, which we replace with a diffusion model estimated from the observations alone by empirical-Bayes expectation-maximization. The resulting posterior is sampled with a guided process whose projection step makes every sample satisfy the balance exactly. On synthetic systems of six to thirty-five bidding zones, built from ENTSO-E resource-adequacy data, the diffusion prior gives the most accurate reconciliation, increasingly so as the system grows. Its credible intervals are calibrated or conservative, and it remains the most accurate under a misspecified noise covariance. Finally, when the generation of entire zones goes unreported, the classical methods fail while the learned prior recovers it from cross-zone structure.

title: SUGARv2: Learning Diverse Visual Humanoid Loco-Manipulation Skills from Synthesized Interaction References
summary: Scaling up visual humanoid loco-manipulation skill acquisition requires reducing the human effort needed as tasks and spatial configurations expand, particularly in demonstration collection and task-specific training design. We present SUGARv2, a unified framework for learning diverse visual humanoid loco-manipulation skills through interaction reference synthesis and a shared training pipeline. To obtain diverse references at low cost, we adapt reusable task templates to different spatial configurations, synthesizing coordinated robot and object motions. To reduce task-specific reward design and training effort, we use reference-based imitation as a common learning objective across tasks. We first train privileged teachers to execute these references, then train visual policies through teacher distillation and reinforcement learning with the same reference-based mimic rewards, using diverse object instances and visual domain randomization to support visual generalization and sim-to-real transfer. Across five humanoid loco-manipulation tasks, SUGARv2 achieves a mean success rate of 91.0% in simulation. Deployment on a real humanoid robot further demonstrates successful sim-to-real transfer for whole-body manipulation. These results demonstrate the framework's potential for learning diverse visual humanoid loco-manipulation skills.

title: Load Balancing with Item Fragmentation and More Bins than Items: Linear-Time and Exact
summary:
We study a fundamental load-balancing problem in which $N$ items of strictly positive integer sizes with total size $W$ must be assigned to $B$ bins, with items allowed to be divided into integer-size fragments across bins. Each bin must receive a load of either $\lfloor W/B \rfloor$ or $\lceil W/B \rceil$, ensuring that the loads of any two bins differ by at most one unit. Under this constraint, the objective is to minimize the maximum number of distinct item fragments placed into any single bin. This problem is NP-hard and there exists an $(\mathrm{OPT}+1)$-approximation algorithm that runs in $O(N \log N + B)$ time [Kobert et al., 2014]. The existing algorithm is employed by several widely used production codes for phylogenetic reconstruction.
  Here, we focus on the case $B \ge N$, that is, bins are at least as numerous as items. This setting arises pervasively in modern parallel and distributed systems, as well as in iterative algorithms that rebalance their workload at every step. In this context, bins are machines or machine cores, and items represent computational tasks (jobs). Our central contribution is a remarkably simple $O(N)$-time algorithm that computes an optimal assignment in this setting; this assignment is encoded using $O(N)$ space. In particular, we prove that an optimum always exists in which every bin receives at most two fragments and provide a characterization of when one fragment per bin suffices. Our result strictly improves the $(\mathrm{OPT}+1)$-approximation of Kobert et al. in the many-bins setting and, together with it, yields a strongly polynomial-time $(\mathrm{OPT}+1)$-approximation algorithm for the general setting, as it removes the dependency on the number $B$ of bins.

title: Thinking Twice: A Sequential Approach to Nudge Towards Reflective Judgment in GenAI-Assisted Decision Making
comments: Full paper accepted and presented at the 20th International Conference on Wirtschaftsinformatik (WI 2025), Münster, Germany. To appear in the conference proceedings (Lecture Notes in Information Systems and Organisation, Springer). This version is the submitted manuscript prior to peer review
summary: Humans increasingly use generative AI (GenAI) for decision-making assistance, yet tend to engage in such situations using quick, intuitive (System 1) rather than deliberate, analytical assessment (System 2) as reflected in Dual Process Theory. Such engagement reduces the effectiveness of human-GenAI interactions and increases associated risks. Our research investigates how to design human-GenAI interactions that promote the transition from System 1 to System 2 thinking in decision-making. Based on the Three-Stage-Model, which suggests humans switch to System 2 when conflicts are detected, we conducted an experiment (n=130) testing sequential human-GenAI interaction as a cognitive forcing nudge during problem-solving tasks. This approach, where humans decide first before receiving AI assistance, enables detection of conflicting decisions. Compared to non-sequential settings (concurrent or no AI assistance), results show the sequential condition significantly enhanced both decision performance and GenAI prompt utilization, providing valuable insights for designing more reflective and thus effective human-GenAI interactions.

title: EGT: Execution-Grounded Traversability through Learned Closed-Loop Trajectory Distributions
summary: Rough terrain traversability is often estimated through point-wise roll, pitch, or force-angle margins along a planned path. However, these metrics are often inaccurate and overly conservative because they ignore how terrain disturbances and low-level controller corrections can affect the vehicle's motions. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Execution-Grounded Traversability (EGT), defined as the probability that a vehicle-controller pair can execute a candidate path while meeting trajectory-level tracking and progress requirements. We estimate EGT by predicting the distribution of closed-loop trajectories using a latent-space flow matching (FM) model conditioned on multi-resolution terrain features and 3D vehicle attitude and wheel-ground contact points prior. Across 650 simulated trials on unseen terrains, EGT reduces safe-path rejection to 2.2% (versus 11.4%-39.5% for pose-margin and force-angle baselines) and unsafe acceptance to 7.7%. Integrated into a receding-horizon sampling-based planner, EGT reduces navigation failure rates by 24-42 and 30-44 percentage points over [1] and [2], respectively, while cutting goal-reaching time by up to 20.5% and 45%. Finally, we demonstrate zero-shot transfer of our simulation-trained model to real-world outdoor experiments.

title: Zero-Shot Weight-Space Programming Across a Difficulty-Graded Ladder of Two-Player Games
summary: Weight-space programming sets every weight of a feed-forward network by hand, from an explicit specification of the desired computation, with no gradient descent and no training data anywhere in the construction. We ask how far a large language model can carry this practice, zero-shot, across games of deliberately increasing difficulty. We design a four-rung ladder (Nim, tic-tac-toe, two sizes of Connect Four, and a chess endgame) spanning four axes of difficulty, and build a second, independent network at each rung, using a structurally unrelated game at matched difficulty, to separate what a rung's finding says about the difficulty level from what it says about the one game used to measure it. Ten networks are built and independently verified. Six admit a complete, non-statistical proof of correctness against an independent oracle. The chess-endgame rung is exact where correctness is cheap, move legality and, in one network, an exact one-ply mate detector, and collapses where it is expensive, composing a multi-move mating plan, from 84.1-100% success at the one-ply tactics it was built to get right down to 0.57-9.13% in full adversarial play; its replicate shows this collapse is an order of magnitude less severe under a shorter required plan and exact rather than heuristic safety checks. The standard-sized rung confirms, by holding hand-set evaluation weights fixed and adding only shallow search, that the remaining gap is an architectural ceiling rather than a matter of engineering effort, and this exact collapse reproduces across two structurally unrelated games. We release all ten networks, their independent oracles, construction-cost measurements, and a cold-prompt protocol for a future cross-model comparison

title: Task-Driven Closed-Loop Design Optimization of Passively Morphing Quadrotors for Contact-Mediated Narrow Gap Traversal
summary: Aerial robots operating in cluttered environments may encounter openings narrower than their nominal width. Existing passively morphing drones reduce their width upon traversal, but they typically involve human-made designs, which can struggle to find the right balance among folding ratio, flight efficiency, and control tracking performance. We introduce a closed-loop design method that jointly optimizes quadrotor geometry and the torque-deflection response of two passively folding arms driven by the success rate in simulation for contact-mediated gap traversal. An optimization algorithm samples candidate designs that are evaluated in a contact-based simulation of the traversal task, where the task success rate is used as a feedback signal to sample progressively better designs over time. The resulting prototype passively reduces its width from 31.3 to 14.1 cm and traverses a 15 cm wide opening at a 2 m/s reference speed. It also tolerates gap approach-angle errors of up to 30 degrees and folds through a 40 cm long confined passage. Compared to a rigid twin, the soft configuration adds only 2 mm of position RMSE and less than 1% electrical power during contact-free flight. These results show that task-driven closed-loop design optimization can produce passively morphing airframes that are compact under contact, tolerant to approach error, and effectively rigid during nominal flight.

title: PHISHREV+: An ASP-Based Post-Hoc Defeasible Machine Learning Framework for Phishing Detection
summary: Phishing website detection remains a critical cybersecurity challenge. Although machine learning classifiers achieve high accuracy on benchmark datasets, they suffer from a fundamental limitation: once trained, their decision boundaries are fixed and cannot incorporate new contextual evidence without retraining the model. This work presents \textbf{PHISHREV+}, a hybrid framework that instantiates the notion of \textit{post-hoc defeasible machine learning}. This framework does not replace the classifier. It treats the initial classifier predictions as defeasible beliefs and revises them through an Answer Set Programming based non-monotonic reasoning(NMR) layer. The framework operates in two phases. In the machine learning phase, four classifiers (SVM, KNN, DT and RF) are trained on the 87 feature benchmark dataset. In the post-hoc NMR phase, four defeasible rules derived from exploratory data analysis of the training set, and validated through Chi-square and Mann-Whitney U tests, formally revise initial predictions. The proposed framework achieves consistent false positive reduction across all our classifiers SVM (41$\rightarrow$39), KNN (47$\rightarrow$46), DT (62$\rightarrow$61), and RF (52$\rightarrow$51) while maintaining complete false negative parity with zero increase overhead. A comprehensive ablation studies across seven rule configurations confirms that the hierarchical combination of all four defeasible rules is necessary to achieve this optimal balance. Instance level explainability is provided through eXplainable ASP (XASP), which generates formal derivation graphs showing which defeasible rules fired and why the initial belief was retracted, a capability absent from all existing phishing detection approaches.

title: FondueQA: A Benchmark for Evaluating Parametric Compensation in Multi-Hop QA
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) show remarkable performance based on parametric knowledge, i.e., their ability to recall facts and associations internalized in a model's weights. However, studying this capability on established multi-hop benchmarks may be complicated by benchmark contamination, as many of these benchmarks have been publicly available long enough to plausibly appear in modern pretraining corpora. As a result, correct answers under missing evidence may reflect either general parametric knowledge or memorization of benchmark-specific instances. To study how models use internal knowledge when retrieval evidence is incomplete, we introduce FondueQA, in which every required multi-hop fact is uniquely localized to a designated evidence document. This enables controlled document-level evidence ablations to study parametric compensation under incomplete retrieval. Our empirical evaluation reveals that parametric compensation strongly depends on both entity popularity and the structural role of missing evidence. Generally, models compensate more successfully for facts involving popular entities. On FondueQA, we show that bridging evidence can be more useful than the answer-bearing document itself. Moreover, models may recall a missing fact in isolation but fail to use it under partial evidence, particularly when the context contains plausible competing entities, which can reduce Exact Match by up to 15 percentage points.

title: AudioSphere: Towards Self-Supervised Spatial Audio Representation Models
comments: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: Recent audio embedding models learn representations that transfer across clip- and frame-level tasks, yet they operate almost exclusively on single-channel signals and are blind to spatial structure. Spatial audio models capture that structure but rely on clip-level supervision or contrastive objectives, yielding embeddings unsuitable for frame-level tasks like sound event detection and localization (SELD). We argue this dichotomy is not fundamental: patch-level spatial self-supervision can jointly learn acoustic and spatial features at both temporal granularities. We introduce AudioSphere, a multi-channel masked autoencoder trained on Ambisonics recordings that reconstructs both spectral content and directional cues via a joint spatiotemporal masking strategy that masks both time-frequency patches and intensity vectors. AudioSphere supports frame-level predictions while producing strong clip-level representations via aggregation. Alongside the model, we release RealSELD, a standardized benchmark for evaluating frozen backbones on real-world multi-channel SELD. AudioSphere enables, for the first time, SELD with a frozen self-supervised backbone, while matching or exceeding prior self-supervised audio embedding models on clip-level classification tasks spanning environmental sound, speech, and music, and on frame-level sound event detection. All code and data are available at https://github.com/labhamlet/AudioSphere and https://huggingface.co/labhamlet.

title: DC-Link Voltage Regulation in a Single-Isolation-Stage Multioutput Solid-State Transformer for Wide-Range DC Outputs
comments: Submitted to IEEE Transactions on Power Electronics (TPEL) for possible publication
summary: Single-isolation-stage solid-state transformers with balancing circuits eliminate an additional downstream dc--dc conversion stage. However, the remaining isolated converters must directly accommodate a wide output-voltage range. This paper investigates variable dc-link voltage operation of a single-isolation-stage multioutput SST to ease this requirement. Coordinated cascaded H-bridge modulation and embedded four-switch balancing circuits support intentionally unequal submodule dc-link voltages, allowing the isolated-converter input voltages to be adjusted according to the output requirements. The achievable voltage range is determined by relating the required balancing power to the BC transfer capability within the available CHB switching windows, subject to modulation and peak and rms current limits. The analysis quantifies the range extension provided by BC operation beyond modulation alone. For a single-phase-shift dual-active-bridge converter, input-voltage following within this range reduces the calculated peak current and extends the ideal zero-voltage-switching region compared with fixed input. Experiments on a six-submodule SST prototype demonstrate unequal dc-link voltage operation and inter-submodule power exchange. Experiments result on DAB demonstrate reduced current stress and improved efficiency with voltage following.

title: Federated Forensics: Jurisdictional constraints as a design driver for multi-agency federated learning
summary: Digital forensic investigations increasingly cross borders, and law enforcement agencies need to build analytical models together without centralizing their data. Federated Learning (FL) keeps data local, yet neither FL nor its frameworks enforce the jurisdictional, governance, and accountability rules that multi-agency forensic work requires. This paper takes a design-first approach to that gap. First, we derive seven requirements that a federated learning system must meet in a forensic setting. Second, we propose Federated Forensics, a three-layer reference architecture whose middle layer, unlike in existing hierarchical FL designs, sits at a jurisdictional border and can use a model update locally while blocking it from crossing that border. Third, we build a prototype of the architecture and test it on a malware-family classification task. In a prototype evaluation, the policy gate blocked every restricted update at the border with zero violations, and restricted-class accuracy rose from 0% under today's compliant alternative to 93.0%, only 4.4 points below ignoring the restriction.

title: Diversity-Aware Client Selection for Communication-Efficient Federated Learning
comments: 4 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Accepted at SNCNW 2026
summary: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed clients without sharing raw data, making it attractive for privacy-sensitive and bandwidth-constrained applications. A practical challenge in deploying FL is reducing communication overhead while maintaining model performance under heterogeneous, non-IID data distributions. Selecting which subset of clients participates in each training round offers a principled way to address both challenges simultaneously, yet its impact on data diversity and representativeness remains underexplored. In this paper, we investigate three client selection strategies, Power-of-Choice, Fisher information, and Centered Kernel Alignment, evaluating them not only by accuracy and convergence, but through the lens of participation diversity using the Gini coefficient and KL divergence. Under non-IID conditions, restricting participation to 15% of clients per round achieves significant communication savings, and when selection promotes diverse and balanced contributions, it also improves generalization over biased alternatives. This work provides a systematic and reproducible analysis demonstrating that diversity-focused client selection renders communication efficiency and model quality complementary rather than competing objectives.
comment: 4 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Accepted at SNCNW 2026

title: AnomSep: Bridging Optimization-Based Separation and Deep Neural Refinement for Anomaly Detection with Listenable Explanations
summary: We propose AnomSep, which combines optimiza-tion-based separation with deep neural refinement to achieve accurate anomaly detection with listenable explanations. Anomaly detection requires no predefined anomalous categories, and understanding the basis for each detection helps security personnel assess the validity of each detection. End-to-end anomaly detectors can achieve high detection accuracy but output only scalar scores, and existing anomalous sound separation methods provide listenable explanations with limited detection accuracy. AnomSep first obtains preliminary normal-sound and anomalous-sound estimates through optimization-based separation using a dictionary learned from normal sounds in the target environment. Deep neural refinement then improves the preliminary estimates in a pretrained audio latent space. The separated anomalous sound serves as the listenable explanation, and its energy determines the anomaly score. Experiments on synthetic mixtures and real mixtures show improved separation quality over baseline separators. AnomSep achieves detection performance competitive with the end-to-end baseline and provides listenable explanations directly linked to each detection decision.

title: An Empirical Study of Issues in GPU Kernel Libraries for LLM Systems
summary:
Behind the expanding use of large language models (LLMs) across application domains lies a growing dependence on specialized GPU kernel libraries. These libraries underpin the correctness and efficiency of training and inference across diverse GPU platforms, implementing attention, GEMM, quantization, and low-precision operators while managing tensor shapes, memory layouts, code generation, and hardware-specific dispatch. Problems at this layer can silently corrupt outputs, hang GPUs, prevent compilation, introduce deployment incompatibilities, or degrade performance, thereby reducing developer productivity and wasting expensive GPU resources.
  We present the first comprehensive empirical study of issues in GPU kernel libraries for LLM systems. We manually analyzed 300 high-quality GitHub issue reports, their discussions, and available fixes from seven representative libraries: FlashInfer, FlashAttention, Triton, CUTLASS, DeepGEMM, xFormers, and bitsandbytes. The analysis characterizes symptoms, root causes, fixes, and testing and debugging practices. Our main findings are: (1) 60.33% of the sampled issues originate in the Compiler and Build System or Runtime Environment dimensions, so validation must cover the deployment and execution stack, not just kernel code. (2) Kernel specialization imposes implicit correctness constraints on tensor shapes, metadata layouts, memory aliasing, and hardware resources. Violations can produce incorrect outputs or launch failures even for supported operations, highlighting the need for explicit contract validation and boundary-case testing. (3) Current testing and debugging practices are often insufficient for identifying low-precision numerical problems and hardware-specific execution failures. We outline research opportunities and tooling directions to support future LLM GPU kernel development.

title: A semi-implicit exactly well-balanced relaxation scheme for the 2d shallow water system
summary: We propose a semi-implicit, exactly well-balanced finite volume scheme for the two-dimensional shallow water equations over a non-flat bottom, aimed at the low-Froude-number regime. The method combines a Suliciu-type relaxation of the pressure with a flux splitting that separates the fast acoustic waves from the slow transport ones: the pressure subsystem is integrated implicitly and the transport subsystem explicitly, so that the time step is no longer restricted by the acoustic stability condition. Written in terms of its Riemann invariants, the pressure subsystem decouples into independent one-dimensional problems along the grid lines, each of them governed by a banded linear system whose bandwidth does not depend on the mesh. The implicit step therefore requires no non-linear solver and costs O(NxNy) operations, regardless of the acoustic Courant number. A two-dimensional exactly well-balanced reconstruction, whose limiter weights are frozen within each time step, preserves this linear structure for the second-order scheme. We prove that both the first- and the second-order schemes preserve water-at-rest equilibria exactly, and we assess them on several two-dimensional benchmarks, where they resolve fine-scale velocity structures on coarse meshes and run up to 8.5 times faster than standard explicit Riemann solvers.

title: Ontology-Driven Control of Conversational Agents with a Use-Case for Job Interview Practice
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been widely used as conversational agents in both domain-specific and open-domain situations. In domain-specific context, it is often necessary to adapt those LLMs to obtain conversations with desired characteristics, whether those apply at the level of each response (e.g. for tone or style) or more globally (i.e. at the level of a conversational strategy). Such adaptations are, however, generally realized in an ad hoc way, through specific, non-reusable, and non-transparent developments. In this paper, we propose an ontology-based approach to design conversational strategies that rely on the desired and measured characteristics of textual utterances in the conversation. Through a use case related to job interview practice, we show how this approach can be used to control LLMs to follow the strategy defined in the ontology. To this end, we automatically fine-tune the LLM to improve its compliance with ontologically-defined conversation characteristics. Our results show that training the LLM from formally defined concepts effectively enhances alignment with the requested characteristics. Hence, this work demonstrates how ontology-guided conversation control can be achieved while taking into account multiple, concurrent conversation aspects that are formally and transparently defined.

title: Safety-Focused Reinforcement Learning Using Risk-Sensitive Coupled Control
summary: This paper investigates the coupled control problem within safety-focused reinforcement learning, addressing the essential challenge of achieving optimal performance while ensuring safety in systems operating within complex environments. We define safety as the requirement to prevent the system from reaching undesirable or hazardous states. We propose a coupled control approach that prioritizes safety by employing effective methods to prevent the system from entering unsafe states while optimizing the performance metric, defined as the average cost. We propose a novel problem transformation that reformulates it into a risk-sensitive problem combined with an average reward criterion. We present a two-timescale Q-learning algorithm where in the faster timescale, the algorithm solves a risk-sensitive control problem to ensure safety, while on a slower timescale, the algorithm focuses on average cost control. We provide theoretical guarantees for the convergence of our algorithms, establishing their significance in ensuring safe, optimal control in dynamic environments. We validated the performance of our approach using GridWorld and CarGoal task in Safety Gymnasium.

title: AutoRefine: Auto-Calibrating Code Judges from Workflow Outcomes
comments: 5 pages, 3 figures, prepared for submission to CAIN 2027 industrial track
summary: LLM judges increasingly serve as quality gates for code changes that have no test oracle, but a judge prompt must be calibrated for its task and recalibrated as the system it judges evolves, while hand labels for the calibration are resource intensive and go stale. Development workflows emit outcome labels for free (tests pass or fail, changes land or are abandoned), but these labels are noisy. We present AutoRefine, a loop that rewrites a deployable judge's prompt to reproduce outcome labels, with an informed teacher that sees the judge's input plus the outcome, explains each label it keeps, and abstains when the outcome cannot be explained from what the judge sees. On a held-out dataset with an execution oracle, calibration raised chance-corrected agreement (Scott's $π$) from 0.36 to 0.60. On a deployed agent's outcome labels, with 25\% flipped at random to introduce noise, the teacher set aside flipped \textsc{fail} labels at more than twice the rate of genuine ones, cutting overall label noise from 25\% to 20\%. Recalibrating that agent's judge using AutoRefine raised its agreement with merge/abandon outcomes on 17 independently held-out diffs from the current workflow ($π$ 0.16 to 0.51); on 16 diffs from older workflows, the previous judge stayed ahead, illustrating the need for recalibration as the agent evolves. By abstaining, the teacher not only removes noisy labels but also flags changes whose outcome the judge's input cannot explain, telling a team when a judge needs better inputs rather than a better prompt.

title: High-order FEEC discretization on 2D and 3D domains with a disk-like coordinate singularity
summary: Tensor-product splines mapped from a square to a disk-like domain form a discrete de Rham complex, but at the coordinate singularity the pushed-forward $0$-, $1$- and $2$-forms are discontinuous, unbounded and not square integrable. Existing polar constructions impose either high-order regularity on the $0$-forms only, or first-order regularity on the whole complex. For general disk-like mappings composed with a smooth diffeomorphism, we construct polar subspaces of all three tensor-product spaces that are conforming, form a cochain complex with the cohomology of the disk, and are $\mathcal{C}^{\mathfrak{r}-m}$ at the center for $m$-forms, for any $\mathfrak{r}$ up to the spline degree, under a compatibility condition between the mapping and the angular basis. The construction enriches the $2$-form space with projected polynomials and lifts them to curl-like $1$-forms by Poincaré-type homotopy operators, which reduce to cumulative sums of radial B-spline coefficients, so that the homotopy identities hold exactly. The same operators yield sparse commuting projections that preserve total flux and circulation, and boundary-compatible homotopies that solve the curl--curl problem with a single mass-matrix inversion. In 3D, the tensor product with a periodic 1D complex carries all properties over to stellarator-like solid tori. Numerical experiments confirm optimal projection accuracy and the predicted regularity, show that the regularity conditions suppress the stiff central modes of the curl--curl operator, allowing more than ten times larger time steps than first-order polar spaces, and that compatible high-order regularity is required for convergent guiding-center orbits near the axis of a discrete vacuum field.

title: MDF++: Visuo-Tactile World Action Model with End-to-end Representation Learning
summary: Recently, world-action models (WAMs) have emerged as a powerful framework for robot manipulation. By jointly modeling action generation and future observation prediction, WAMs can act and anticipate the outcomes of the actions. However, existing WAMs typically rely on frozen pretrained encoders trained with reconstruction, which may not produce representations well suited for robot control. In this paper, we tackle the problem of learning physicallygrounded, control-relevant representations for WAMs. We propose MDF++, a visuo-tactile world-action model that learns latent representations of multisensory observations end-to-end with a diffusion backbone. While naive joint training can lead to feature collapse, MDF++ introduces a multi-task learning strategy that leverages cross-modal correlations to learn task-relevant representations. We evaluate MDF++ on a suite of contact-rich manipulation tasks, including realworld bolt screwing and nut mating, and show that it outperforms WAMs built on frozen pretrained representations by up to 50%. Additional videos are available on our website: jointmdf.github.io.

title: Orthogonal Norm Growth in Two-Tower Retrieval: A Popularity Mechanism for Unified Discovery
comments: 6 pages, 1 figure. Accepted at USRW 2026 (non-archival), co-located with ACM RecSys 2026. Supplementary material included as an ancillary file. Workshop: https://usrw-workshop.github.io/2026/accepted-papers.html . Code: https://gitlab.com/wrapper228/usrw_pb
summary: Unified search and recommendation systems may update the same item vectors from both interaction streams. We study how repeated updates can increase an item vector's norm and affect retrieval under an unnormalized dot product. A cosine-only loss makes the output gradient perpendicular to the current item vector - tangent to its constant-norm sphere. Training changes encoder parameters, however, so the realized item-vector movement need not remain tangent. We derive sufficient conditions under which it does; every nonzero update then increases squared norm by its squared length. When the tasks share an item encoder, sequential updates from both can accumulate in the same norm, which raw-inner-product serving can expose for either task. This conditional result is not a theorem about joint SGD. Controlled ablations test these conditions. On MovieLens 32M and Amazon Books, accumulated tangent movement accompanies frequency-norm association and additional head-item exposure under raw-dot rather than normalized-item ranking. In a nonlinear tower combining a per-item ID vector with a shared content encoding, active item movement remains near-tangent. We separate its norm change into the ID-update contribution and other output changes, then use a matched training intervention that removes immediate norm growth caused by the ID-row update. The intervention reduces norm-related exposure but also recommendation utility, so it is diagnostic rather than a proposed mitigation. Our logs are recommendation-only: the formulation supplies a shared-representation audit, while prevalence in joint traffic remains open.

title: Bridging Spiking and Continuous Dynamics in Spiking Neural Networks: A Muscle-Inspired Model
summary: Transforming the spike trains produced by spiking neural networks (SNNs) into continuous signals through biologically inspired mechanisms remains an open challenge in generative and regression tasks. In biological systems, a similar transformation occurs when muscles integrate neural spikes to produce smooth, coordinated movements. Inspired by this mechanism, we introduce a muscle-response model, a biologically motivated dynamical layer that converts spike trains into continuous representations. Our approach uses second-order dynamics to model the temporal integration of spiking activity. We investigate how the number of spiking neurons and temporal resolution affect the quality of the generated signals in a text-to-speech task, showing that increasing representational capacity has a greater impact than increasing temporal resolution under the evaluated configurations. Furthermore, an analysis of the learned dynamics reveals that, without explicit constraints on the response type, most neurons converge toward non-oscillatory behavior. These results demonstrate the potential of biologically inspired dynamical decoders for bridging spiking neural computation and continuous signal generation.

title: Multilingual Artificial Datasets for AI-Driven Cardiology: the CliTe and ParaCliTe corpora
summary: Background and Aims. Comparable, multilingual, validated cardiology corpora are critical to advance trustworthy natural language processing (NLP) models for cardiology but such resources are scarce due to privacy concerns. This study aimed to cover this gap by presenting suitable artificial corpus creation guidelines and by releasing 3 multilanguage corpora. Methods. Following purpose-specific publicly-available corpus construction guidelines, cardiologists from 7 European hospitals generated artificial clinical records in Czech, Dutch, English, Italian, Romanian, Spanish and Swedish, ensuring clinical diversity and sex balance, resulting in the CliTe corpus. A CliTe subset underwent a multi-stage manual translation into the other 6 languages, resulting in the parallel ParaCliTe corpus, while the remaining reports were automatically translated, constituting ParaCliTe Silver. Results. CliTe is a collection of 699 artificial cardiology reports, mostly outpatient notes (340 documents), discharge reports (263), and inpatient notes (89), describing fictional patients with ischaemic heart disease (199 patients), heart failure (188), and valvular disease (79), among others. ParaCliTe contains reports from 94 fictitious patients, each available in seven languages with sentence-level alignment, resulting in 658 documents. The corpus mainly comprises discharge reports (322 documents), and outpatient (196) and inpatient (140) notes, describing patients with heart failure (399 documents), ischaemic heart disease (287), and valvular disease (238). Empirical results illustrate the utility of ParaCliTe and highlight the limitations of state-of-the-art NLP models adapted to the cardiology domain. Conclusions. The creation of multilingual, equitable and realistic corpora of artificial patients capable of strengthening NLP performance for cardiology is feasible when supported by detailed guidelines.

title: Towards an Autonomous AI Steward for Large-Scale Physics Experiments: Integrating Causal Diagnostics, RAG, and Conformal Prediction
comments: 4 pages, 1 figure, 2nd International Conference on AI for Science (AI4Sci2026), 5-9 October 2026, Mainz, Germany (PoS)
summary: Long-term particle physics experiments face critical operational challenges: monitoring non-stationary machine data streams and preserving tacit expert knowledge. We present the "Helmholtz Co-Pilot," a hybrid Multi-Agent System (MAS) acting as an autonomous experiment steward. The system can be triggered interactively by human operators or autonomously by an asynchronous causal diagnostics engine that runs independently of the MAS reasoning core. Continuously monitoring live hardware streams such as data acquisition and slow control, this engine performs dynamic causal discovery to trace cascading alarms back to their root causes and applies adaptive model selection to keep forecasts reliable across shifting machine states; upon detecting an anomaly, it hands a structured diagnostic report to the MAS. The reasoning layer itself relies on a high-throughput C++ core and a Python edge architecture orchestrating a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of specialized ReAct workers. It integrates a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) backbone for institutional memory and leverages conformal prediction to bound its evidence-based recommendations with mathematical coverage guarantees. This extended abstract outlines the architecture, the integration of software-enforced Human-in-the-Loop (HitL) guardrails, and ongoing shadow-testing within the KATRIN experiment.

title: A Stochastic Latent Variable Generalization of Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures
summary: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) predict the latent embedding of a target signal from a context signal, with an auxiliary variable z conditioning the predictor. Despite its prominent role in the original JEPA blueprint, the content of z has been carried by a fixed deterministic token in every prior instantiation, collapsing the genuinely multi-modal distribution over plausible completions to a point estimate. We present S-JEPA, which realises z as a proper stochastic latent variable for masked image prediction: a learned posterior infers z from context and target during training, while a learned context-conditioned prior approximates the distribution of plausible completions at inference, with no decoders and no reconstruction. In its deterministic limit the objective reduces to the I-JEPA loss in functional form, generalising that objective rather than strictly containing the I-JEPA model. Our central finding is that stochasticity adds capabilities, error-correlated predictive uncertainty and diverse completions, at no cost to representation quality: under matched architectures and schedules S-JEPA improves over the deterministic I-JEPA baseline and exceeds LeJEPA at matched architecture, while additionally producing spatially structured uncertainty maps and semantically diverse completions, neither of which the deterministic predictor produces.

title: T2I Models Rarely Invert Negation but Often Fail to Suppress Negated Concepts: Benchmarking Negation Suppression in Text-to-Image Generation
comments: Accepted at WACV 2027. Code and data: https://github.com/IAB-IITJ/T2I-NSI
summary: Text-to-image diffusion models often fail to suppress explicitly negated concepts, such as a lamp for "a desk without a lamp." We introduce T2I-NSI, a benchmark and metric for measuring negation sensitivity in text-to-image generation. It pairs each negated prompt with a canonical positive counterpart and factorizes negation by linguistic form (lexical/semantic, morphological, syntactic) and target type (objects, attributes, relations, compositions, and nested cases). The benchmark contains 759,869 paired prompt atoms over a 5,082-object catalog, with 916,272 images (911,982 open-weights, 4,290 closed-source), scored by a Basic CLIP estimator and a Robust ensemble of CLIP, VQA and open-vocabulary detection. Negation sensitivity is low: open-weights generators score NSI <= 0.038, while GPT-Image-1.5 and Gemini-2.5-Flash-Image reach about 0.09. The dominant failure is under-suppression rather than misdirection. Inverse interpretation is essentially absent (0.00% across over 450K atom-model evaluations), whereas models render the concept under both prompts on 8-19% of atoms and only partly suppress it on a further 9-25%; most remaining atoms are too weakly rendered to label. A blinded human study (420 atoms, nine annotators) corroborates the near-absence of inversion and the high persistence rate, and a matched-prompt comparison shows the open-versus-closed gap (~3.5x) is not a prompt-generator artifact. Code and data: https://github.com/IAB-IITJ/T2I-NSI

title: An Optimal Power-Flow Grouping Topology for Single-Isolation-Stage Multi-Output Solid-State Transformers
comments: 13 pages, 19 figures. Submitted to IEEE for possible publication
summary: Electric-vehicle dc fast-charging stations and data centers require multiple high-power dc outputs with independently varying demands. Conventional multi-output solid-state transformers typically establish a common dc bus and use downstream dc/dc converters for port-level regulation and, where required, galvanic isolation. A single-isolation-stage solid-state transformer can eliminate this additional high-power interface stage by directly forming multiple isolated outputs from its submodule dc/dc stages. However, because one submodule is generally insufficient for an individual output port, multiple submodules must be connected in parallel, while inter-submodule balancing circuits redistribute power under unbalanced loading. The submodule grouping therefore determines the internal balancing-power paths. Sequential grouping can create long transfer paths and accumulated balancing power, increasing current stress and losses. This paper proposes an optimal power-flow grouping topology that interleaves submodules assigned to different output ports, thereby localizing power redistribution and reducing the power processed by the balancing circuits. Analytical models quantify the required balancing power and its reduction relative to sequential grouping. A coordinated submodule-bypass strategy is also developed, and the remaining output-power capability under different fault scenarios is evaluated. A six-submodule prototype validates the proposed topology. Under the same highly unbalanced operating conditions, the proposed topology reduces the maximum submodule dc-link voltage difference by 63\% and the peak balancing current by 14.5%, while improving the measured efficiency by approximately 5.6% at rated power. Stable post-fault operation is also experimentally demonstrated.

title: Wake 5: A Python Framework for Solidity Testing, Fuzzing, and Static Analysis
summary: Smart-contract fuzzers differ by an order of magnitude in throughput and by design in how they construct inputs, yet published comparisons rarely separate the two. We present Wake 5, an open-source Python framework for Solidity testing, fuzzing and static analysis, and use it to locate the binding constraint of stateful smart-contract fuzzing. Wake 5 replaces the JSON-RPC connection to an external node with an in-process EVM (revm) and exposes its static analysis to language-model agents through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. On the Daedaluzz maze benchmark (153 reachable assertions, guard constants below 2^32), Wake 5 executes 29,931 transactions per second, on par with Foundry (30,186) and 11.5x faster than Echidna (2,600). In eight-hour campaigns, however, the three tools plateau at medians of 75, 71 and 70 assertions, and their union reaches 93. We show that Wake's integer generator places 51% of its probability mass below 2^32 and that, once shallow assertions are exhausted, the generator prior rather than throughput bounds every tool. A harness written by a language-model agent, which derives inputs with a constraint solver, reached all 153 assertions in each of five campaigns executed by Wake, in 33 to 79 minutes. A complementary ablation in an agentic audit of a production Go codebase found that static-analysis tools improved recall for none of three models, raised precision for all three, and increased language-model cost by up to 12.7%. We discuss correlated oracles and non-deterministic completion, and argue that the fuzzer's role is shifting from search to execution.

title: Interpretable Context-Aware Multi-Label Retinal Classification with Dual-Hub Heterogeneous Graph Neural Network
summary: Multi-label retinal screening requires capturing co-occurring pathologies and clinical context, yet standard multimodal fusion remains opaque. We propose a dual-hub heterogeneous graph neural network (GNN) that couples spatial fundus features and structured clinical covariates through cross-modal message passing while providing inherent interpretability. Rather than relying on post-hoc saliency approximations, our architecture exposes multi-level decision pathways during forward aggregation: spatially biased self-attention captures lesion-level patch interactions, while modality-specific graph attention coefficients explicitly quantify the contribution of visual regions and clinical risk factors to each disease node. Evaluated on the BRSET dataset (16,266 photographs from 8,524 patients), the proposed model achieves 76.1% Macro-AUPRC across seven conditions, matching or exceeding image-only (75.9%) and ResNet-50+MLP fusion (75.9%) baselines, with largest contextual gains in macular edema (+3.5%) and diabetic retinopathy (+2.1%). Codebase is available at: https://github.com/proshanto-c/ca-mlc-refactor.

title: Asymmetric Correspondence Learning for Lexical and Style Embeddings: Interpreting Latent Space via Acoustic Features
comments: Accepted to Spoken Language Technology 2026. 6 pages
summary: Self-supervised speech embeddings jointly encode lexical, speaker, and prosodic information, complicating feature isolation. We introduce Asymmetric Correspondence Learning (ACL), distilling HuBERT features into separate Acoustic Word Embeddings (AWEs) and Acoustic Style Embeddings (ASEs) via a split-latent correspondence bottleneck. Through probing and clustering evaluations on single-word utterances, we demonstrate that substantial variance from extrinsic sources remains encoded within each latent space, despite linear probing indicating the information has been stripped. Whilst the AWE space exhibits cohesive lexical clustering (AP$\approx$0.90, Fisher$\approx$6.28), linear probing on the ASE space achieves 97.9\% speaker accuracy across a diffuse topology (Fisher$\approx$1.01), yet preserves substantial lexical variance (Fisher$\approx$0.86) that remains linearly unrecoverable (0.17\%). To explain these findings, we apply group-level permutation feature importance over eGeMAPS acoustic features, finding that AWEs partition by vocal tract filters and ASEs by $F_0$ dynamics. These findings suggest that standard diagnostic benchmarks may be insufficient for verifying feature isolation, as substantial speech structure can be retained even when it remains entirely hidden from probes.
comment: Accepted to Spoken Language Technology 2026. 6 pages

title: Verification of Security Properties of Cryptographic Protocols
summary: Developing cryptographic protocols that are free from vulnerabilities is very challenging, as evidenced by numerous design flaws and implementation bugs in widely used protocols. Recent work has leveraged model checking to generate negative test cases, that is test cases that include the behavior of Dolev-Yao attacker. In this paper, we address the problem of analyzing execution traces produced by testing protocol implementations with such negative test cases. We propose a method for detecting violations of security properties by model-checking execution traces. Our approach employs a model checker based on DLTL, a Linear Temporal Logic with freeze operators, and supports automation of the testing process through pre- and post-processing steps. These steps, respectively, bridge the gap between different levels of abstraction and synthesize the results produced by the model checker.We present experimental results as a proof of concept for the feasibility of the proposed method.

title: Keyline Detection with YOLO: Runway Perception for Vision-Based Aircraft Landing
summary: Modern object detectors can predict keypoints as per-object geometric features, but keypoints are inherently vulnerable to occlusion and truncation.
